newsitem.title: CROATIA: U.S. presses Croatia, Serbia on human rights.
newsitem.headline: U.S. presses Croatia, Serbia on human rights.

text.p: Croatia and Serbia must improve their human rights record and cooperate with a U.N. war crimes tribunal if they want economic and political aid from the United States, a senior U.S. official said on Tuesday.

John Shattuck, assistant Secretary of State for democracy and human rights, flew into Croatia on Tuesday after visiting Bosnia. Shattuck's three-day visit to former Yugoslavia will include a trip to the Serbian capital Belgrade on Wednesday.

He met Croatian Foreign Minister Mate Granic earlier to discuss the rights of minorities, freedom of the press and Zagreb's cooperation with the International Crimes Tribunal for former Yugoslavia (ICTY).

"Croatia's commitments to protect rights of minorities, full freedom of press and to fully cooperate with the ICTY have to be realised over time for stronger U.S. relations with Croatia," Shattuck told reporters after the meeting.
"(That) includes stronger relations on the economic front, military, as well as political front," he said. "In particular I emphasized the cooperation with the tribunal."
Shattuck said the question of minority Serbs, most of whom fled to Serbia ahead of a Croatian army offensive last year, was a "major human rights issue".
Croatia has baulked at letting the refugees back home and is accused of persecuting or even murdering those who stayed behind.
The ICTY has indicted over 70 people from former Yugoslavia, most of them Bosnian Serbs. Eighteen Bosnian Croats were charged with genocide against Moslem civilians.
The tribunal holds only seven suspects in its custody.

Only one of the Croat indictees handed himself over to the tribunal. The extradition of another one is to take place soon, while all other indictees are still at large, some of them presumably living in Croatia.
Shattuck said Granic had reiterated Croatia's pledge to cooperate, but refused to say if Zagreb had promised to take any concrete action soon.

Shattuck is due to meet Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic in Belgrade on Wednesday to "discuss the same issues - cooperation with the tribunal, turning over (of the indictees) who are in Serbia and freedom of press".
He said Milosevic would be offered prospects of further assistance, access to international financing, the World Bank and the United Nations.
"The U.S. is prepared to support all of that if there is full cooperation with the tribunal and progress in human rights in Kosovo," he said.
Kosovo is Serbia's southern province notorious for violations of human and ethnic rights against its Albanian majority.
